definitions.explanation: A hood attached to a jacket, parka, or hoodie. Pulled up over the head against rain or cold.

definitions.gloss: food (esp. in compounds and brand-style names)
definitions.explanation: Food, used mostly in fixed compounds such as ファストフード, ペットフード, ベビーフード. Rare on its own.

examples.japanese: {雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}ってきたのでフードをかぶった。
examples.english: It started to rain, so I pulled up my hood.

examples.japanese: このパーカーはフードに{裏起毛|うらきもう}が{付|つ}いていて{暖|あたた}かい。
examples.english: This hoodie has a fleece-lined hood, so it's warm.

examples.japanese: ペットフードを{買|か}いに{行|い}く。
examples.english: I'm going to buy pet food.

examples.japanese: ファストフードは{手軽|てがる}だが{栄養|えいよう}バランスが{悪|わる}い。
examples.english: Fast food is convenient but nutritionally unbalanced.

examples.japanese: {離乳食|りにゅうしょく}にベビーフードを{活用|かつよう}している{家庭|かてい}も{多|おお}い。
examples.english: Many households make use of baby food when weaning their child.

notes:
Two unrelated English loanwords spelled the same in katakana: "hood" and "food." Context — usually whether the word stands alone or appears in a compound — makes the sense clear.

SENSE 1 (hood):
- フードをかぶる: to pull up a hood
- フード{付|つ}き: hooded (e.g. フード{付|つ}きのパーカー)
- フードを{外|はず}す: to push the hood back / take the hood off

SENSE 2 (food, compound use):
- ファストフード: fast food
- ペットフード: pet food
- ベビーフード: baby food
- ドッグフード: dog food
- フードコート: food court

Used by itself, フード is almost always taken to mean "hood." When the meaning is "food," speakers normally use {食|た}べ{物|もの} or {食品|しょくひん} instead.
